explanations.answer: The prophets' words and the Lord's commands
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Peter wants them recalling what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through their apostles. That's two things in one reminder: the prophets' words and the Lord's commands. Peter packs a lot into one verse, and it's all right there in 2 Peter 3:2.

explanations.answer: Their fathers' stories and the elders' rules
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a solid answer, friend, but it's not what Peter says. He points to what was foretold by the holy prophets. He also points to what was commanded by our Lord and Savior, and he says it came through their apostles. So the commands are the Lord's, not the elders'.

explanations.answer: The kings' records and the priests' laws
explanations.explanation: Close to a real-sounding list, but Peter doesn't mention kings or priests here. He says the reminders are about what was foretold by the holy prophets. The other half is what our Lord and Savior commanded through their apostles. Prophets and apostles, friend. That's the pair.

Right on the money, baker. Peter says the scoffers will ask, “Where is the promise of His coming?” I think it sounds like someone staring at the oven and asking “Is it done yet?” every thirty seconds. Peter says scoffers like that will come in the last days, and he wants believers ready for them.

This one is true, friend. Peter really does say the scoffers will ask, “Where is the promise of His coming?” It's right there in 2 Peter 3:4. The scoffers are the ones asking it, and Peter says it before they even open their mouths.

Exactly. The scoffers say, “…everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation.” They say it right after asking where the promise of His coming is. Peter doesn't go along with them, and he's about to say why.

That's not what the scoffers say, friend. They say everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation. Changes is the opposite of that. Peter spends the next verses answering what they say.

Not quite, baker. The scoffers don't say anything about things weakening. They say everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation. They think the world just keeps rolling along the same as always.

That's it, baker. Peter says the world of that time perished in the flood. He ties it to water: the earth was formed out of water and by water, and the world of that time perished through that same water. Peter says the scoffers deliberately overlook this when they say everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation (2 Peter 3:4-6).

An earthquake would shake things up, friend, but it's not what Peter names. He says the world of that time perished in the flood. He connects it to the water the earth was formed out of and by. No earthquake in this verse at all.

Hold on, baker, nobody's rationing cookies in this verse. Peter points to water, the same water the earth was formed out of and by. Through it, he says, the world of that time perished in the flood. That's the answer.

Yes, baker. Peter says the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire by that same word. The world of that time perished in the flood, but this present one is being kept for fire. Peter says it's being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men (2 Peter 3:7).

Water is a fair guess, friend, because Peter just talked about the flood. But he says the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire. The flood belongs to the world of that time. Fire is what this present world is kept for.

Rest sounds nice, baker, like the end of a long day of baking. But Peter says the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire. They're being kept for the day of judgment. That's what the word of God has set aside for them.

explanations.answer: A day is like a thousand years to Him
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Peter says, “With the Lord a day is like a thousand years…” He wants believers to keep hold of that and not let it escape their notice. It's the Lord's view of time, and it's different from ours (2 Peter 3:8).

explanations.answer: A year is like a watch in the night to Him
explanations.explanation: That's a good-sounding line, friend, but it isn't what Peter says here. In this verse he says a day is like a thousand years with the Lord. That's the one thing he doesn't want them to miss. Stick with Peter's own words on this one.

explanations.answer: A day is like a single breath to Him
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't compare a day to a breath, baker. He says, “With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.” He gives it both ways, and a breath isn't in either one. That's the one thing he doesn't want escaping their notice (2 Peter 3:8).

Yep, baker. Peter says it both ways: “…a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.” The comparison runs in both directions. Time just doesn't work for the Lord the way it works for us (2 Peter 3:8).
This one is true, friend. Peter says, “…and a thousand years are like a day.” That's the second half of the same verse. He gives the comparison flipped around so nobody misses it.

That's it, baker. Peter says the Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you. So what looks like slowness is patience. That's Peter's own word for it in 2 Peter 3:9.
Silent is a tempting word, friend, especially to a scoffer asking where the promise is. But Peter says the Lord is patient with you. That's the word he picks. He doesn't say silent.

Angry isn't Peter's word, baker. I think a long wait can sound like a short fuse to a scoffer, but Peter says the Lord “…is patient with you…” He goes on to say the Lord is not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. So the patience is aimed at people turning around, not at anyone getting what's coming to them.

That's right, baker. Peter says the Lord is not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. Nobody is left out of that "everyone." That's what the Lord's patience is aimed at (2 Peter 3:9).

Offerings aren't in this verse, friend. Peter says the Lord is “…not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.” Nothing in that sentence asks anyone to bring something. Repentance is about turning around, not carrying something to the altar, and the Lord wants everyone to get there (2 Peter 3:9).

Feasts aren't in this verse, baker. Peter says the Lord is not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. That's the thing He wants instead of anyone perishing. Everyone coming to repentance.
You got it, baker. Peter says the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. He doesn't tell us the day or the hour here. The picture is that it arrives without a warning (2 Peter 3:10).

A mist drifts in nice and gentle, friend, but that's not Peter's picture. He says the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. Then he goes straight to the roaring heavens and the fire. Nothing misty about that.
A sunrise at least comes with a little glow first, baker. But Peter says the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. That's the comparison he picks in 2 Peter 3:10.
Peter says the opposite, friend. He says the earth and its works will be laid bare. Laid bare means out in the open, not hidden. So this one is false (2 Peter 3:10).

Right, baker. Peter says the earth and its works will be laid bare. Nothing stays hidden. He says it right after the heavens disappear with a roar and the elements are destroyed by fire (2 Peter 3:10).

explanations.answer: Holy and godly in how they live
explanations.explanation: That's the answer, baker. Peter says, “You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness” He's talking about how they live, not just what they believe. The question comes first, then the answer, both in 2 Peter 3:11.

explanations.answer: Quiet and careful with their money
explanations.explanation: Careful with money is wise, friend, and the bills always come due. But it isn't what Peter says. He says they ought to conduct themselves in holiness and godliness. That's how he answers his own question.

explanations.answer: Sharp and quick in every debate
explanations.explanation: Sharp and quick is a fun answer, baker, but Peter doesn't say it. His answer is that they ought to conduct themselves in holiness and godliness. He's pointing at how they live. Winning arguments isn't in that verse.

explanations.answer: A new heaven and a new earth
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Peter says, “But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth…” After all the fire talk, this is the good part. He says it's in keeping with God's promise (2 Peter 3:13).

explanations.answer: A return to the garden of Eden
explanations.explanation: That's a lovely thought, friend, but Peter doesn't say it. He says, “But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth…” The promise is God's, and what it points to is a new heaven and a new earth. Eden isn't named in this verse (2 Peter 3:13).

No temple in this verse, baker. After all that talk of fire, Peter turns with a “But” and says, “But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth…” That one little word flips the mood, like the oven timer finally going off. The new heaven and new earth are what he names (2 Peter 3:13).

That's it, baker. Peter says the new heaven and new earth are a place “…where righteousness dwells.” It's a place where right living has a home. That's the world believers are looking forward to (2 Peter 3:13).

Sorrow isn't in this verse, friend. Peter says the new heaven and new earth are a place “…where righteousness dwells.” Dwells means it lives there, like it's home. So what he names is righteousness, not sorrow (2 Peter 3:13).

Silence does sound peaceful, baker, but Peter doesn't go there. He says “…where righteousness dwells.” Righteousness means being right, in how people live and in standing with God. After all that fire and melting, he doesn't promise a quiet place. He promises a place where what is right has a home (2 Peter 3:13).

That's right, baker. Peter says to make every effort to be found at peace, and then adds “…spotless and blameless in His sight.” That's how he wants them found while they wait. He says it to believers he calls beloved (2 Peter 3:14).

Those sound serious, friend, but Peter doesn't use them here. He says to make every effort to be found at peace, spotless and blameless in His sight. Fasting isn't in the verse. Neither is the word watchful.
Bold and outspoken is a fun pair, baker, but it's not on Peter's list. He wants believers found at peace, spotless and blameless in His sight. That's what he asks them to make every effort toward.
That's the answer, baker. Peter says, “Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation…” The patience he talked about earlier isn't just waiting around. It brings salvation (2 Peter 3:15).

Delay is a fair-sounding word, friend, but Peter doesn't say it. He says, “Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation…” Earlier he said the Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness (2 Peter 3:9). So where some see slowness, Peter points to salvation.

Doubt isn't where Peter lands, baker. He says, “Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation…” The scoffers ask where the promise is, but Peter points to what the waiting does. It brings rescue, since the Lord is not wanting anyone to perish (2 Peter 3:9). Doubt only sees the clock, but Peter sees people being saved.

That's right, baker. Peter says that Paul, whom he calls our beloved brother, also wrote to them with the wisdom God gave him. Peter says Paul wrote about the same matters. He tells them in 2 Peter 3:15.
James is a good guess, friend, since he wrote a letter too. He's the one who calls himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1). But Peter doesn't name James here. He names Paul.
Jude wrote a letter as well, baker. He calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James (Jude 1:1). But Peter doesn't name him in this passage. The writer Peter names is Paul.
Yep, baker. Peter says, “Some parts of his letters are hard to understand…” He says that about Paul's letters. Peter says ignorant and unstable people distort those parts (2 Peter 3:16).
This one is true, friend. Peter says some parts of Paul's letters are hard to understand. He says so right in 2 Peter 3:16. Then he adds that ignorant and unstable people distort them.

That's it, baker. Peter says, “…be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless…” He says it because they already know these things. Knowing the truth and guarding it go together (2 Peter 3:17).

Peter doesn't tell them to hide, friend. He says to be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless. That's a different thing than keeping to themselves. Guarding is the word he uses.

That would be a LOT of answering, baker. But Peter doesn't tell them that. He says to be on their guard so they won't be carried away by the error of the lawless. That's his instruction in 2 Peter 3:17.

That's right, baker. Peter says to be on guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless “…and fall from your secure standing.” The believers have a secure standing, and Peter wants them to keep it. He says it in 2 Peter 3:17.
Peter doesn't talk about a place in town, friend. He says they could fall from their secure standing. That's what the error of the lawless could carry them away from. The standing is what's at stake.

Family favor isn't in this verse, baker. Peter's worry is that the error of the lawless could carry them away. What they could fall from is their secure standing. That's why he says to be on guard (2 Peter 3:17).

Yes, baker. Peter says, “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.” After the warning, this is his final instruction. It's about growing in Jesus Christ, and it's right there in 2 Peter 3:18.
Rest sounds nice, friend, especially after all that fire. But Peter says to grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Growing is the word he uses in 2 Peter 3:18.

Waiting does come up earlier, baker, when Peter says they anticipate these things. But in this verse he says to grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. That's the instruction for this blank. Grow is the word.
